title: Decoding gene responsiveness to synthetic chromatin reader-actuators with multi-modal epigenomic profiling.
authors: Kim, Seong Hu; Enwerem-Lackland, Isioma; Williams, Natecia L; Fisher, Rachel; Plaisier, Christopher; Haynes, Karmella A
abstract: Cell identity is regulated by chromatin states that encode gene regulatory memory and shape responses to new inputs. To investigate how chromatin context influences inducibility in differentiated cells, we employed engineered synthetic reader-actuators (SRAs), fusion proteins containing the polycomb chromodomain (PCD) that binds H3K27me3. In MCF7 breast cancer cells, we mapped PCD-fusion occupancy by ChIP-seq and used RNA-seq to identify temporally resolved gene activation patterns. ChIP-seq profiling and machine learning models (MLM) demonstrated that PCD-fusion binding was predicted primarily by the absence of H3K4me3 or H3K9ac enrichment, suggesting selective accessibility at enhancers and chromatin transition zones. Among genes with SRA-enriched enhancers, the SRA-induced subset was distinguished by promoter features including bivalent histone modifications and enrichment of transcription factors NEUROD1 and MTA1. Collectively, our results demonstrate that SRA responsiveness depends on a specific chromatin signature beyond H3K27me3 alone. This study demonstrates the power of SRAs to dissect inducible chromatin features in their native genomic context, and suggests that epigenetically repressed regions in differentiated cells can retain regulatory plasticity.

title: Enterococcus mundtii regulates SfCYP6B39 expression to modulate chlorantraniliprole resistance in Spodoptera frugiperda.
authors: Ren, Zhijie; Hu, Ziwei; Bao, Yueyue; Qin, Wu; Qin, Jiangmei; Wan, Hu; Tan, Huihua; Chen, Hongsong
abstract: Microbiota-mediated adaptation is increasingly recognized as an important driver of insecticide resistance. Here, we demonstrate that gut symbionts promote chlorantraniliprole resistance in Spodoptera frugiperda through transcriptional regulation of host detoxification pathways. Resistant populations exhibited a distinct gut microbial community dominated by Enterococcus mundtii, accompanied by elevated cytochrome P450 (P450) activity and widespread upregulation of detoxification genes. Disruption of the gut microbiota reduced resistance, suppressed P450 activity, and downregulated multiple P450 genes, whereas recolonization with E. mundtii SC1 restored these effects. Functional analyses employing RNA interference and transgenic Drosophila melanogaster identified SfCYP6B39 as a key gene contributing to resistance. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations further revealed that chlorantraniliprole can stably bind to SfCYP6B39. Mechanistically, E. mundtii SC1 promotes SfCYP6B39 overexpression via the transcription factors CncC and BR-C, forming a microbe-host regulatory axis that links symbiont presence to detoxification gene activation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that gut symbionts enhance insecticide resistance through transcriptional reprogramming of host detoxification networks, providing mechanistic insight and suggesting microbiome-targeted strategies for sustainable pest management.

title: Shikonin triggers apoptosis in lung adenocarcinoma through the FHL2-FOXO1 signaling axis.
authors: Chen, Shiqun; Zhou, Meirong; Zhang, Wen; Zhong, Jiyong; Han, Wenqian; Wang, Zhaoxuan; Wang, Shiqing; Gu, Chundong; Yu, Zhenlong; Zhao, Shilei
abstract: BACKGROUND: FHL2 is an oncogenic scaffold protein that is overexpressed in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), making it a promising therapeutic target. SHK, a natural naphthoquinone, exhibits antitumor activity, but its molecular mechanism in LUAD, particularly its relationship with FHL2, remains unclear. AIM OF THIS STUDY: The present study aimed to define the effects of SHK on NSCLC and identify the potential underlying molecular mechanisms. METHODS: The anti-tumor effects of SHK were evaluated in LUAD cell lines (A549andH1299) and a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model using CCK-8, colony formation, Transwell, and flow cytometry assays. Integrated proteomics, bioinformatics, molecular docking, and cellular thermal shift assays (CETSAs) were employed to identify the direct target of SHK. The underlying mechanism was investigated through co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), Western blotting, qRT-PCR, cycloheximide (CHX) chase assays, and immunofluorescence/immunohistochemiscal (IF/IHC) staining. RESULTS: In both in vitro and PDX models, SHK potently inhibited LUAD growthand metastasisand induced cell death. At the molecular level, FHL2 was identified as a direct target of SHK. The direct binding of SHK to FHL2 promoted its proteasomal degradation, thereby disrupting the FHL2-FOXO1 complex. The dissociation of this complex increased FOXO1 acetylation and promoted its nuclear translocation, leading to the subsequent activation of the caspase cascade and apoptosis. CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate a novel signaling pathway through which SHK inhibits LUAD: by directly targeting FHL2 for degradation, SHK disrupts the FHL2-FOXO1 complex, which activates FOXO1-mediated transcription and triggers apoptosis. This study not only provides mechanistic insight into the antitumor function of SHK but also identifies the FHL2-FOXO1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for LUAD.

title: scHGNN: A single-cell gene regulatory network inference method based on heuristic graph neural networks.
authors: Zhang, Tianjiao; Teng, Xiaopeng; Zhang, Hongfei; Zhao, Zhongqian; Li, Yang; Dong, Benzhi; Wang, Guohua
abstract: The construction of gene regulatory networks based on single-cell transcriptomics (scRNA-seq) data provides crucial technical support for decoding cell fate determination mechanisms at the single-cell level, elucidating molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression, and developing targeted therapeutics. Existing methods for constructing GRNs often rely excessively on gene expression features, struggling to achieve an effective balance between local direct regulatory signals and global multi-step regulatory pathways. This imbalance results in insufficient utilization of topological information within the network structure. Therefore, this study proposes a heuristic graph neural network-based GRN inference model (scHGNN). scHGNN integrates multi-order neighbor topological information into learnable weights through unified heuristic matrix and link prediction modules, thereby balancing local and global regulatory relationships. This approach effectively fuses gene expression features with network structural information to achieve precise inference of latent regulatory links within gene regulatory networks. Across GRN inference tasks using benchmark networks of varying gene scales and diverse origins, scHGNN consistently outperforms existing mainstream methods on key evaluation metrics. Furthermore, in target gene prediction cases for key transcription factors such as TP53, OTX2, and FOXP1, the model achieved validation rates as high as 76%-84% in the hTFtarget database. This not only supports its accuracy in identifying known regulatory relationships but also indicates its potential to identify high-confidence candidate regulatory interactions for further biological investigation. Collectively, these results demonstrate that scHGNN holds significant application value in elucidating gene regulatory mechanisms and exploring the molecular basis of related diseases.

title: Design of Wheat Protein-Derived Keap1-Targeting Antioxidant Peptides: Integrating Intelligent Screening, ProteinMPNN-Guided Sequence Optimization, and TAT-Fused Delivery.
authors: Yu, Tianfei; Lin, Qian; Sun, Zheng; Deng, Amin; Na, Kai; Lu, Ting; Zhang, Li; Yu, Chao; Li, Xiangyu; Guo, Xiaohua
abstract: Wheat gliadin-derived peptides show promising antioxidant potential, but their target-guided discovery remains challenging. Here, we established a computation-driven pipeline for Keap1-targeting antioxidant peptides. From 2798 virtual oligopeptides generated using our Peptide_MDI platform, KCENEECTFP and RELVNSTCFA were selected through multitier screening and molecular dynamics simulations. KCENEECTFP exhibited antioxidant activity and modulated the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway in H2O2-stressed IPEC-J2 cells. Structure-guided ProteinMPNN optimization yielded SCDCPSCLYP, which showed enhanced radical scavenging activity, antioxidant enzyme responses, and regulation of Keap1-Nrf2-related genes. SCDCPSCLYP also promoted Nrf2 nuclear translocation and attenuated p65 activation. Surface plasmon resonance confirmed direct Keap1 binding (KD = 7.25 muM), while the cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) supported Keap1 target engagement in cells. N-terminal TAT fusion further improved cellular uptake and antioxidant efficacy. These findings demonstrate an integrated strategy combining target-guided screening, structure-informed optimization, target validation, and intracellular delivery for the rational development of wheat gliadin-derived antioxidant peptides.

title: Boereguasins A-D, Cytochalasins from Boeremia exigua with Differential MAPK/NF-kappaB Inhibition.
authors: Tian, Chun; Shi, Bao-Bao; Ma, Qin; Liu, Qing; Feng, Meng-Lin; Wei, Yue-Ping; Han, Shu-Yu; Ai, Hong-Lian; Liu, Ji-Kai
abstract: Four unprecedented cytochalasins, boereguasins A-D (1-4, respectively), were purified from the endophytic fungus Boeremia exigua. Structurally, compound 1 contains an adenosine moiety and features a novel bridged 5/6/13/5/6/5 ring system. Compound 2 represents the first cytochalasin with an odd-numbered carbon chain (19 carbons), which is presumably assembled via the fungal polyketide synthase pathway from an unusual propionyl-CoA starter unit. Compound 3 incorporates an unusual 15-membered carbocyclic ring, while compound 4 possesses a novel 5/6/14/6 tetracyclic scaffold. The structures were established by comprehensive spectroscopic analysis, ECD calculations, and DP4+ analysis. Compound 2 exhibited potent anti-inflammatory activity in LPS-induced RAW264.7 macrophages, significantly reducing NO, TNF-alpha, IL-6, and PGE2 levels. It suppressed the MAPK/NF-kappaB signaling pathway by inhibiting the phosphorylation of ERK, JNK, IkappaBalpha, and p65 and downregulating iNOS and COX-2 expression. Transcriptomic and docking studies confirmed that 2 targets key regulators and stably binds to the active pockets of TPL2 and NF-kappaB p65. In vivo, 1 and 2 reduced foot edema and inflammatory cytokines, with no acute toxicity observed.

title: Interpretable Protein-Nucleic Acid Binding Site Prediction via Domain-Guided Multimodal Learning.
authors: Xi, Wenyu; Wang, Ruheng; Ye, Xiucai; Sakurai, Tetsuya; Wei, Leyi
abstract: Accurate identification of protein-nucleic acid binding sites is essential for elucidating molecular mechanisms and for enabling structure-based drug discovery. Existing computational approaches struggle to jointly model sequence, structure, and domain knowledge, which limits both predictive accuracy and interpretability. We present BiMTBind, a domain-guided multimodal deep learning framework that integrates bidirectional state-space modeling with Transformer-based attention for residue-level binding site prediction. The model explicitly incorporates protein-domain annotations as biological priors to guide attention toward functionally relevant regions. Multi-source featurescontextual embeddings from protein language models and handcrafted structural descriptorsare fused via a learnable gating mechanism that adaptively weights each modality. This design enables the model to capture both global dependencies and local context. Extensive evaluations across diverse DNA and RNA benchmarks show that BiMTBind consistently outperforms state-of-the-art sequence- and structure-based methods on multiple metrics, including F1, MCC, and AUC. Case studies further show that domain-guided attention improves interpretability by aligning predicted binding residues with annotated functional domains. These results highlight the effectiveness of combining biologically informed priors with deep multimodal representation learning, offering a scalable and generalizable approach for protein-nucleic acid binding site prediction.

title: Promoter Engineering in Yeast Cell Factories: Strategies, Applications, and Perspectives.
authors: Bai, Zhenzhen; Jiao, Tian; Darvishi, Farshad; Chu, Haodong; Wang, Zheng; Shi, Shuobo
abstract: Yeasts serve as premier eukaryotic hosts for microbial cell factories, enabling the production of recombinant proteins, biofuels, and high-value natural products. Precise transcriptional control is paramount for balancing complex metabolic pathways and maximizing target product yields. Promoters, as the key regulatory elements governing transcription initiation, have thus become a focal point of metabolic and synthetic biology engineering. This review surveys promoter architecture, function, and engineering in yeast. It outlines promoter structure, from core elements to upstream regulatory sequences, and reviews current and emerging strategies for discovery, optimization, and de novo design, including random mutagenesis, combinatorial assembly, rational design based on transcription factor binding sites, intron-mediated enhancement, cross-species approaches. Importantly, this review highlights the rapidly growing role of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) in promoter engineering, from predictive modeling of promoter strength to in silico generation of synthetic variants. Special emphasis is placed on synthetic promoter engineering to yield tunable and inducible toolkits. The review also highlights applications in yeast cell factories, such as metabolic pathway optimization, dynamic regulation, high-throughput strain screening, and recombinant protein production. By summarizing these recent advances, it serves as a practical resource for researchers aiming to achieve precise metabolic control and improve bioproduction outcomes in yeast.

title: A Single Mutation Enhancing the DNA-Binding Affinity of Cra Redirects Metabolism for High-Yield Succinate Production in Escherichia coli.
authors: Wei, Wan-Fang; Wang, Ruo-Lin; Huang, Ying; Tang, Meng-Ying; Jia, Kai-Zhi; Wang, Wei-Ping; Zhao, Wei; Liu, Xiao-Nan; Zhu, Li-Wen
abstract: Rational engineering of transcription factors is an attractive strategy to modulate microbial metabolism. This study demonstrated its effectiveness through a key mutation (R60A) in the understudied linker region of the global transcription factor Cra. Transcriptional and enzymatic analyses revealed that R60A upregulated multiple genes and enhanced several key enzyme activities in central carbon metabolism, including the direct Cra targets pck and aceB, which were selected for further mechanistic investigation. In vitro binding assays confirmed that R60A bound to the promoter regions of these genes with enhanced affinity. Molecular docking analysis predicted that the top-ranked binding poses of the WT and R60A complexes differ in DNA placement, with an altered set of predicted hydrogen-bond contacts. This mutation altered the central carbon metabolism, leading to improved CO2 fixation and succinate biosynthesis. Coupled with an optimized exponential feeding strategy that precisely controlled the specific growth rate, this approach achieved a high succinate titer of 100.8 g/L. Our work suggests a possible role for linker-mediated geometric modulation of DNA binding by Cra and presents an integrated metabolic and process engineering strategy for efficient succinate production.

title: beta-Hydroxybutyrate Exacerbates Klebsiella pneumoniae-Induced Inflammatory Injury and Milk Synthesis Impairment via the GPR109A/NF-kappaB Signaling Axis.
authors: Wang, Jue; Yuan, Changning; Cai, Siyi; Ni, Luanyu; Liu, Kangjun; Guo, Long; Cui, Luying; Dong, Junsheng; Li, Jianji; Zhu, Guoqiang; Wang, Ran; Zhang, Lili; He, Tao; Meng, Xia; Wang, Heng
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Ketotic cows exhibit a heightened mastitis risk through an unknown mechanism. This study investigated the influence of beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHBA) on mastitis development. Mammary tissues from ketotic cows with mastitis showed more severe pathological damage and suppression of lactation-related genes. BHBA pretreatment further increased NF-kappaB pathway activation, facilitated expressions of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and suppressed lactation proteins in Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae)-infected BMECs, thereby exacerbating inflammatory injury and milk synthesis impairment. Molecular docking, DARTS, and CETSA assays confirmed that BHBA directly bound to GPR109A. GPR109A knockdown blocked the activation of the NF-kappaB pathway, alleviated inflammatory injury, and mitigated milk synthesis impairment. Meanwhile, similar findings were identified with PTX (an inhibitor of GPR109A) treatment. These findings elucidated the role of BHBA and its endogenous receptor GPR109A in K. pneumoniae-induced inflammatory injury and milk synthesis impairment, which provided valuable insight for understanding the interplay between metabolic imbalance and postpartum mammary health.

title: Immunomodulatory Effects of Galleria mellonella and Alphitobius diaperinus Protein Digestates Generated Using a Modified INFOGEST Protocol - In Vitro and In Silico Evidence.
authors: Ma, Zidan; Boesch, Christine; Mondor, Martin; Sanchez-Velazquez, Oscar Abel; Hernandez-Alvarez, Alan Javier
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Insect-derived peptides have attracted increasing attention due to their potential health-promoting properties. This study investigated peptides released from Galleria mellonella (W) and Alphitobius diaperinus (B) proteins following a modified static INFOGEST protocol. Digestion-derived peptides were identified by LC-MS/MS and evaluated for anti-inflammatory activity using in vitro assays, bioinformatic prediction, and molecular docking, focusing on IKK-beta as a key regulator of the NF-kappaB pathway. At 500 mug protein/mL, W-I2h and B-I2h reduced NF-kappaB reporter activity by 28.7% and 53.5%, respectively, and decreased nitric oxide production by 31%. Digestates also reduced IL-6, TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, and IL-1beta secretion at selected concentrations and decreased IL-6 and IL-1beta mRNA expression. Conversely, 25 mug protein/mL increased IL-1beta secretion by 109.4% and 102.1%, respectively. Increased HO-1 and gammaGCS transcripts suggested modulation of Nrf2-responsive gene expression, although pathway activation was not confirmed. These findings demonstrate concentration-dependent immunomodulatory effects and identify candidate peptides for future validation.

title: Carnosol Accelerates Pressure Ulcer Healing via Keap1-Nrf2/HO-1-Mediated Mitochondrial Quality Control.
authors: Dong, Sheng; Ge, Xin; Lu, Xinyu; Meng, Jian
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Pressure ulcer pathogenesis involves ischemia-reperfusion-induced oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Carnosol, a rosemary-derived diterpene with antioxidant properties, was investigated for its therapeutic potential in tissue repair. Carnosol pretreatment protected HaCaT keratinocytes from oxidative injury by enhancing viability, reducing reactive oxygen species and apoptosis, and promoting migration. Network pharmacology identified the Keap1-Nrf2/HO-1 axis as a candidate pathway; molecular dynamics simulations predicted and surface plasmon resonance demonstrated direct carnosol-Keap1 binding. Nrf2 silencing, HO-1 inhibition, or Keap1 overexpression attenuated carnosol's protective effects. Mechanistically, carnosol-induced HO-1 restored DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission and PINK1-Parkin-dependent mitophagy, maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis via mitochondrial quality control. In vivo, topical carnosol accelerated wound closure, improved histological repair, and upregulated Nrf2/HO-1 in a mouse pressure ulcer model, with superior histological and angiogenic outcomes versus intraperitoneal delivery. Carnosol facilitates pressure ulcer healing via Nrf2/HO-1-driven mitochondrial quality control, supporting development as a topical therapeutic candidate.

title: Targeting the "Undruggable" STAT3 DBD: Free-Energy Perturbation-Guided Design of Covalent Micheliolide Derivatives Targeting Cysteine 367.
authors: Deng, Yangping; Bian, Hengwei; Zhang, Fengyuan; Lin, Jianping; Li, Hongbo; Chen, Yue; Li, Jing; Guo, Jianshuang; Fu, Haohao
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains a highly lethal malignancy, largely due to persistent STAT3 signaling that sustains cancer stem cells (CSCs) and drives therapeutic resistance. Conventional inhibitors targeting the conserved SH2 domain of STAT3 have exhibited limited selectivity and efficacy. Here, we report that micheliolide (MCL), the active metabolite of the clinical-stage candidate ACT001, inhibits STAT3 through Cys367 (C367)-dependent covalent engagement within the DNA-binding domain (DBD)-a residue unique to STAT3 among STAT family members. This specific modification disrupts STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activity prior to any detectable inhibition of upstream JAK phosphorylation, a finding that suggests that STAT3 inhibition is not primarily driven by upstream kinase blockade. Guided by covalent docking, R-group enumeration, and relative binding free-energy calculations via free-energy perturbation (FEP), we have designed and synthesized a series of MCL analogs. These derivatives retain comparable antiproliferative potency but exhibit markedly improved physicochemical properties, including enhanced kinetic aqueous solubility and optimized lipophilicity. Microscale thermophoresis confirms C367-dependent binding, while microsecond-scale molecular dynamics simulations and pair-interaction energy analyses highlight stable complexes in which electrostatic interactions predominate, with major contributions from key residues (Lys365, Val366, and Ile368). This study establishes C367 as a druggable covalent site in the historically challenging STAT3 DBD, validates FEP-guided optimization of covalent inhibitors, and identifies compound 16 as a promising next-generation lead with a superior drug-like profile for targeting STAT3-dependent cancers. All in all, these findings provide a foundation for advancing selective STAT3 DBD inhibitors toward clinical translation.

title: Random Hybrid Polypeptides Regulate Immune Signaling through Promiscuous and Dynamic Interaction Landscapes.
authors: Chen, Haolin; Zhou, Haisen; Jin, Tianyi; Zhang, Zhihui; Zhao, Zhenzhong; Cai, Haoran; Yu, Xiaoman; Liu, Hong; Chen, Shi; Li, Chuang; Yan, Xuehai; Wu, Guangqi; Qi, Miao; Liu, Lixin; Chen, Yongming; Lu, Hua
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: We developed a high-throughput synthesis and screening workflow combined with machine-learning-assisted optimization to identify functional compositions for immunomodulation in random hybrid polypeptides (RHPs). Using a selenium-containing polypeptide platform, we constructed a nucleoside-functionalized RHP library incorporating nucleoside, cationic, and anionic interaction motifs. Machine-learning-assisted optimization of this library identified a lead RHP, termed IDP-IMP (intrinsically disordered protein-inspired immunomodulatory polypeptide), that suppresses CpG DNA-Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling with limited cytotoxicity. Rather than acting as a conventional strong nucleic acid scavenger or TLR9 antagonist, IDP-IMP showed moderate binding/association with both CpG and TLR9 through different side chain compositions, leading to reduced intracellular CpG-TLR9 colocalization. Across the polymer library, stronger CpG binding did not necessarily correspond to greater inhibitory activity, indicating that CpG binding alone did not predict functional activity. In a collagen-induced arthritis rat model, IDP-IMP attenuated inflammation and joint pathology without detectable systemic toxicity. These findings demonstrate a high-throughput approach for identifying statistical polymer compositions perturbing CpG-TLR9 signaling. The results highlight the importance of IDP-like weak, multivalent, and dynamic interactions in immunomodulation.

title: Investigating potential molecular mechanisms linking 6PPD-quinone exposure to Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: A network toxicology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation study.
authors: Yang, Bin; Wang, Xiangjin; Zhuo, Li; Chen, Yutong; He, Qiansong
abstract: As an emerging pollutant derived from tire rubber, 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) has raised public health concerns due to widespread environmental exposure; however, its potential toxicological effects on avascular tissues such as intervertebral discs remain unclear. This study integrated network toxicology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation to investigate the potential mechanisms linking 6PPD-Q exposure to intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). ADMET toxicological predictions indicated high model-predicted probabilities for SR-MMP and SR-ARE activation. Through multidimensional database integration, 59 common targets potentially associated with 6PPD-Q and IVDD were identified. Protein-protein interaction network analysis further identified five hub genes: PTGS2, MMP2, SMAD3, RELA, and GSK3B. Functional enrichment analysis suggested that these targets were mainly involved in AGE-RAGE, PI3K-Akt, MAPK, TNF, and IL-17 signaling pathways, collectively implicating oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis. Molecular docking showed favorable predicted binding between 6PPD-Q and the five hub proteins, with RELA exhibiting the most favorable docking score (-8.82 kcal/mol). A subsequent 100-ns MD simulation of the 6PPD-Q-RELA complex showed relatively stable RMSD, Rg, and SASA profiles and a concentrated low-energy conformational basin, supporting its dynamic stability under the simulated conditions. Collectively, these computational findings suggest potential molecular links between 6PPD-Q exposure and IVDD and provide hypotheses for subsequent experimental validation.

title: Single-Atom Modification Enables Reversal of Degradation Selectivity between NSD2 and GSPT1.
authors: Shen, Weizhong; Liu, Yihan; Liu, Lianchao; Liu, Yingfan; Zhang, Yan; Chen, Yihan; Wang, Lei; Zhou, Zhiyi; Zhang, Angela; Shen, Hui; Zhou, Fengtao; Huang, Weixue; Ren, Xiaomei; Parolia, Abhijit; Xu, Yong; Zhou, Yang; Wang, Zhen; Chinnaiyan, Arul M; Ding, Ke
abstract: Both NSD2 and GSPT1 represent compelling targets for anticancer drug discovery. Herein, we carried out single-atom modification of LLC0424, an NSD2 degrader with GSPT1 neosubstrate engagement, to yield two structurally analogous molecules with divergent modes of action: 424-ND, an NSD2-selective degrader, and 424-GD, a GSPT1-selective degrader. 424-ND drove selective NSD2 degradation and suppressed androgen receptor (AR) signaling in prostate cancer cells. 424-GD induced selective degradation of GSPT1 and upregulated the integrated stress response markers ATF4 and ATF3. Biolayer interferometry revealed distinct ternary complex cooperativity profiles in the presence of NSD2 or GSPT1, which directly correlate with the observed biased degradation activity. Molecular dynamics and metadynamics simulations showed that the compounds adopt distinct low-energy conformational ensembles with different spatial orientations, likely underlying their divergent cooperativity and selectivity. These findings demonstrate that minimal structural alteration permits precision control over degrader target selectivity while furnishing selective chemical probes for NSD2 and GSPT1.

title: Impairing Golgin-45 transcription factor activity unleashes malignant secretion in lung cancer.
authors: Wu, Chao; Kumar, Abhishek; Wang, Shike; Zhao, Weina; Xi, Yuanxin; Wang, Jing; Jain, Abhinav K; Russell, William K; Guo, Hou-Fu; Tan, Xiaochao; Kurie, Jonathan M
abstract: Golgin-45 (G45) is a coiled-coil protein that transits reversibly between the Golgi and nucleus. In the Golgi, G45 serves as a tether for effectors of a pro-tumorigenic secretory program, but its nuclear role remains unclear. Here, we report that, upon entering the nucleus, G45 functions as a basic leucine zipper transcription factor. From genomic mapping, RNA-sequencing, and functional validation studies, we identify G45-binding sites and show that nuclear G45 can function as a transcriptional activator or repressor, a versatility enabled by phase separation into nuclear bodies enriched in transcriptional co-regulators. In lung cancer models, Golgi-docking reinforces, whereas nuclear translocation opposes, pro-tumorigenic activity of G45. Nuclear G45 incorporates into dimeric transcription factors that silence pro-tumorigenic secreted cargos. Epigenetic events in lung cancer degrade nuclear G45 and sequester G45 in the Golgi, which unleashes malignant secretion. Thus, inter-organelle transitions govern a G45-dependent secretory axis that drives lung cancer progression.

title: 5-Hydroxytryptamine 6 Receptor Antagonism Ameliorates Depression-Like Behaviors in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Rats with Potential Involvement of the MEF2C/NF-kappaB Pathway.
authors: Xu, Yi-Fan; Shan, Ling; Wang, Zhi-Hao; Sun, Meng-Han; Mai, Ling-Ling; Lodder, Thijs; Zheng, Qi-Si; Huang, Bin
abstract: This study aimed to investigate whether 5-HT6 receptor (5-HT6R) antagonism could ameliorate epilepsy-associated emotional and behavioral disturbances in rats with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and to explore its potential association with the MEF2C/NF-kappaB pathway. Thirty rats were randomly divided into normal control (NC) group, Model group and 5-HT6R group. The TLE model was established using lithium chloride-pilocarpine. The rats in 5-HT6R group were treated with 5-HT6R antagonist SB271046. Behavioral tests were conducted to evaluate anxiety- and depression-like behaviors associated with epilepsy. Levels of inflammatory factors, 5-HT and KYN in hippocampal tissues were detected by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Neuronal cell death in brain tissues was assessed by TUNEL staining, and the protein expressions of MEF2C and NF-kappaB p65 were measured by Western blotting. Molecular docking between SB271046 and MEF2C/NF-kappaB p65 was performed using AutoDock 4. In addition, JASPAR database was used to analyze the putative binding of CREB1 to MEF2C promoter. Rats in the Model group exhibited significant epilepsy-associated anxiety- and depression-like behaviors, accompanied by aggravated inflammation, decreased MEF2C protein expression and increased NF-kappaB p65 protein expression. Treatment with SB271046 significantly ameliorated these behavioral abnormalities and inflammatory responses, and was associated with upregulated MEF2C protein expression and downregulated NF-kappaB p65 protein expression. KEGG enrichment analysis suggested the involvement of NF-kappaB pathway in TLE. Molecular docking revealed potential interactions between SB271046 and MEF2C/NF-kappaB p65. 5-HT6R antagonist SB271046 may alleviate epilepsy-associated emotional and cognitive disturbances, potentially through neurostabilizing and anti-inflammatory effects linked to modulation of the MEF2C/NF-kappaB pathway. These mechanistic associations remain preliminary and warrant further validation using targeted gain- or loss-of-function approaches.

title: Targeting NCAPG with Arundanine Suppresses Neutrophil/NET-Mediated Immune Evasion and Enhances CD8(+) T Cell Function in Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
authors: Gu, Xuyu; Lu, Dongning; Deng, Ming; Ge, Tao; Jin, Kaiqi; Xu, Xinnan; Xu, Li
abstract: Non-SMC condensin I complex subunit G (NCAPG) is implicated in tumor progression and TGF-beta pathway activation, yet its roles in oncogenesis and immune modulation within the lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) microenvironment remain largely unexplored. Here, we used bioinformatics analysis to identify key upregulated genes in LUSC and assessed the effects of NCAPG and its upstream regulator E2F transcription factor 8 (E2F8) on malignant phenotypes via gain- and loss-of-function assays in NCI-H226 and NCI-H1703 LUSC cell lines, with in vivo efficacy validated using KLN205 cell isografts and NTCU-induced primary LUSC mouse models. Neutrophil polarization, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and CD8(+) T cell cytotoxicity was analyzed in co-culture systems and tumor tissues. Arundanine was identified as a potential NCAPG inhibitor via molecular docking and tested as monotherapy or in combination with anti-PD-1 therapy. We found that NCAPG was significantly upregulated in LUSC, and NCAPG depletion markedly impaired LUSC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion while promoting apoptosis. Mechanistically, NCAPG activated TGF-beta signaling, which drove pro-tumor N2 neutrophil polarization and induced NETosis; these NETs upregulated PD-L1 expression on tumor cells and suppressed the expansion and cytotoxic function of CD8(+) T cells. E2F8 was found to transcriptionally activate NCAPG by directly binding to its promoter. Furthermore, Arundanine destabilized NCAPG protein, suppressed TGF-beta-mediated NET formation, and potentiated anti-PD-1 therapy to significantly prolong survival in LUSC models. Collectively, the E2F8/NCAPG axis promotes LUSC progression by orchestrating a TGF-beta-driven immunosuppressive microenvironment, and targeting NCAPG with Arundanine represents a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome immune evasion and sensitize LUSC to PD-1 blockade.

title: Targeting the Parkinson's disease interactome: a systems pharmacology and molecular dynamics investigation unveils Berberis aristata-derived phytoconstituents as potential modulators of tyrosine hydroxylase and p53: a systems and molecular dynamics investigation.
authors: Chatterjee, Aniruddha; De, Abhijit
abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) is a heterogeneous disorder of complex etiology involving the loss of motor activities. These findings included mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation of the brain; the deposition of certain proteins within dopaminergic neurons. Berberis aristata DC, a plant traditionally used as anti-diabetic herb in Ayurvedic system of medicine. It has also been found to have neuro-protective properties. We first screened a broad range of the photochemical and then used network pharmacology to calculate association between the target proteins and proteome components. The map of protein-protein interactions produced a large overlap between plant targets and the known PD biomarkers; and the hub proteins, TP53, tyrosine hydroxylase, DRD2, MAOB, and CASP3 were highly central and showed central function in the pathophysiology of PD. Molecular docking demonstrated high binding affinities, especially between the compound meratin and the DNA-binding area of the TP53, and quercetin and the catalytic site of tyrosine hydroxylase. Integrated systems bioinformatics workflow was implemented. The stability of these complexes at long time was verified by molecular dynamics simulations at 100 ns. The functional enrichment analysis identified participation in dopaminergic synaptic signaling, apoptotic mechanisms, and neurotrophin-mediated mechanisms. Predictions of pharmacokinetics showed that key alkaloid constituents were able to traverse through the blood-brain barrier and displayed a low toxicity level. Comprehensively, these results underpin the traditional use of Berberis aristata DC, suggesting its potential to modulate dopamine transmission and apoptotic repression, and making it a good candidate in multi-target Parkinson disease treatments.

title: Deciphering fibroblast and myeloid-cell states in keloids: an integrative analysis identifies ANKRD1 as a ferroptosis-related candidate gene.
authors: Xie, Rongrong; Yao, Wanting; Chen, Peipei; Zhou, Xianying; Lin, Xingong; Jia, Xinyu; Lin, Yuyang; Yu, Zehao; Tang, Shijie; Chen, Caixiang; Chen, Penghong; Wang, Chaoyang
abstract: BACKGROUND: Keloids are fibroproliferative skin disorders characterized by persistent extracellular matrix deposition and limited treatment options. Ferroptosis has been implicated in fibrosis, but the molecular basis of ferroptosis-related changes in keloids remains unclear. METHODS: Fibroblast-derived bulk transcriptomic datasets (GSE44270 and GSE145725) were integrated to identify differentially expressed ferroptosis-related genes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis and machine-learning algorithms were used to identify candidate hub genes, which were evaluated in an external fibroblast dataset (GSE7890). Whole-tissue single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE191067) were used to characterize fibroblast and myeloid-cell states in keloid and normal-skin samples. Candidate regulatory relationships and potential ANKRD1-binding compounds were assessed in silico. Clinical tissue specimens were used for histological and protein-expression validation. RESULTS: A total of 163 differentially expressed genes were identified, and integration with 1,318 ferroptosis-related genes prioritized ANKRD1 as a candidate hub gene. ANKRD1 showed an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve above 0.80 in the external validation dataset and was positively associated with YAP1 expression in fibroblast-derived bulk transcriptomic data. Single-cell analysis identified a ECM-remodeling fibroblast state and three myeloid-cell states: inflammatory macrophages, resident-phagocytic macrophages, and DC-like myeloid cells. The ceRNA analysis identified a putative NEAT1/MALAT1-miR-493-5p-ANKRD1 regulatory axis. Molecular docking, molecular-dynamics simulation, and ADMET profiling prioritized oleanolic acid and quercetin as candidate ANKRD1-binding compounds. Histological analyses showed excessive collagen deposition and increased ANKRD1 protein expression in keloid tissues. CONCLUSION: ANKRD1 is a ferroptosis-related, fibroblast-associated candidate gene in keloids. The single-cell data describe fibroblast and myeloid-cell states in the keloid microenvironment. The proposed regulatory axis, candidate compounds, and potential role of ANKRD1 in fibroblast-myeloid interactions require further spatial and functional validation.

title: Disentangling polymer confinement from specific-folding interactions reveals the drivers of Escherichia coli chromosome organization.
authors: Delafrouz, Pourya; Nesterova, Tanya; Harris, Frances E; Farooq, Hammad; Du, Lin; Liu, Jian; Ma, Ao; Xiao, Jie; Liang, Jie
abstract: The three-dimensional organization of the bacterial chromosome is critical for gene regulation. Chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) has enabled genome-wide mapping of chromosomal folding, yet ensemble-averaged contact maps entangle biologically specific-folding interactions (SFIs) with nonspecific polymer compaction and mask single-cell heterogeneity. Here, we developed a polymer-based simulation framework in Escherichia coli to address these limitations. We found that a null model of 300 000 random polymer configurations recapitulated the global chromosomal organization observed in Hi-C data, establishing that most Hi-C signals reflect generic polymer behavior in a confined volume. Contrasting null-model predictions with experimental Hi-C data isolated a small subset of SFIs (<7%) and generated a specific-fold ensemble of 20 000 single-cell conformations that reproduced chromosomal interaction domains and single-cell heterogeneity. SFIs were enriched in the ter region, reduced nucleoid accessibility, colocalized with cryptic prophages, and depleted in positively supercoiled regions. H-NS and MatP emerged as major chromosome-wide and local determinants of SFIs, respectively. Furthermore, high-SFI regions correlated with stress-adaptive genes, whereas low-SFI regions harbored housekeeping genes. Together, our results established that a small number of biologically encoded SFIs superimposed on a polymer background shape the E. coli chromosome and gene expression, providing a quantitative framework for dissecting chromosome architecture and function.

title: On Organic-Molecule and Peptide Non-Covalent Inhibitors of the TP53-MDM2/MDMX Interaction: An Inside View From the Interaction Energy at Residue-to-Residue Level.
authors: Pietra, Francesco
abstract: Depletion of the tumor-suppressor TP53 is known to open the door to cancer and, after 30 years of research, no remedy has been approved. When TP53 depletion is due to trapping by MDM2, a key requisite for non-covalent inhibitors is high affinity for MDM2 (and also for the MDMX analog, which plays an indirect role in depleting TP53). While inhibitor performance has always been measured by the binding energy, the present work offers a deeper view by evaluating the interaction energy and its electrostatic and vdW components at residue-to-residue level. In the absence of suitable experimental methods, the task was addressed using unrestricted MD and QM-MM, including all inhibitors that are currently in clinical trials, and for which the static structure at high resolution has been made available. It has emerged, in the framework of weak, dispersion-driven interactions that rarely exceed 6 kcal/mol, and with water solvation playing a major role, where the inhibitors bind better and where repulsions arise. In this scenario, a better pattern of interaction energies emerged with stabilized peptides than with organic-molecule inhibitors. All that should help designing the next generation of inhibitors.

title: Deep dynamical models of single-cell multiomic velocities predict loss-of-function and rescue perturbations in B cells.
authors: Karbalayghareh, Alireza; Pelzer, Benedikt; Chin, Christopher R; Melnick, Ari; Barisic, Darko; Leslie, Christina S
abstract: Here we present DynaVelo, a generative neural ordinary differential equation model that learns the joint dynamics of gene expression and transcription factor (TF) motif activity from single-cell multiome data. DynaVelo learns a functional form of the vector field, such that the model can be perturbed in silico and not only used to draw trajectories. We show that DynaVelo recovers the bifurcating in vivo dynamics of wild-type murine germinal center (GC) B cells and reveals how these dynamics change under heterozygous loss of epigenetic regulators Arid1a and Ctcf. In silico perturbation yields dynamic and cell-state-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) that recover known TF-to-gene edges in the wild-type GC GRN and predicts those that are disrupted in mutants. Perturbing Arid1aHet GCs in silico identified Ctcf, Stat3 and Bcl6 as rescue targets for Arid1a loss. In vivo experiments in double-heterozygous mice confirmed rescue of the Arid1aHet dark-zone phenotype in all three cases, and multiome profiling of Arid1aHet;CtcfHet GCs validated the predicted shift toward wild-type dynamics.

title: CCAN forms the spherical shell-like structure in interphase kinetochores.
authors: Sakai, Yuji; Ariyoshi, Mariko; Hirano, Yasuhiro; Mahana, Yutaka; Suzuki, Aussie; Hirota, Toru; Tachikawa, Masashi; Fukagawa, Tatsuo
abstract: The kinetochore is an essential structure for the faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The 16-protein complex known as the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) localizes the centromere throughout the cell cycle and forms the basis of the kinetochore. Although cryo-electron microscopy has provided a structural model of an individual CCAN unit, how multiple CCAN units are organized within cells remains unclear. Here, using in silico and in vivo analyses, we demonstrate that multiple CCAN units form a spherical shell-like structure in interphase DT40 kinetochores. CENP-T and CENP-N localize to the CCAN shell, whereas the CENP-C cupin domain clusters at the center. Molecular dynamics simulations of CCAN assembly suggest that CENP-C-DNA interactions constrain the orientation of CCAN units, supporting a spherical shell-like organization via CENP-C oligomerization. Super-resolution imaging reveals the spherical shell-like structure at DT40 kinetochores, and CENP-C knockout or expression of a CENP-C DNA binding deficient mutant abolishes the structure, consistent with the simulation-derived model. These findings provide important insights into the spatial organization of functional kinetochores within cells.

title: Protocol for live-cell imaging and analysis of NF-kappaB localization and target gene transcription in Drosophila S2 * cells.
authors: Nawar, Noshin; Rits, Emma; Wunderlich, Zeba
abstract: NF-kappaB transcription factor (TF) activation is heterogeneous across identically stimulated cells, shaping innate immune responses. Here, we present a protocol to quantify this heterogeneity in live Drosophila melanogaster S2 * cells using dual reporters of NF-kappaB (Relish) subcellular localization and downstream transcription. We describe steps for reporter cell line generation, immune stimulation and time-lapse confocal imaging, and machine-learning-based single-cell analysis to classify signaling behaviors and predict transcriptional responses. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Nawar et al.(1).

title: Oleanolic Acid Alleviates Diabetic Nephropathy by Inhibiting Ferroptosis Involving the Activation of the NRF2/HO-1 Pathway.
authors: Wu, Gongyu; Wang, Yu; Guan, Yue; Gao, Changjiu; Chen, Peijian; Sun, Xueqing; Liu, Xuping; Guan, Huilin
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Oleanolic acid (OA), a pentacyclic triterpenoid found in agricultural products such as grapes and olives, exhibits potential in alleviating diabetic nephropathy (DN). We validated its renoprotective effects using high-fat diet/streptozotocin (HFD/STZ)-induced diabetic mice and high glucose-stimulated HK-2 cells. Network pharmacology predicted ferroptosis and the NRF2/HO-1 axis as key targets, which was supported by molecular docking and dynamics simulations indicating stable binding. Mechanistically, OA treatment upregulated the NRF2/HO-1 pathway, which was associated with the inhibition of ferroptosis horizontal line evidenced by suppressed lipid peroxidation and iron overload, improved mitochondrial function, and the regulation of key proteins (e.g., upregulating GPX4 and the iron-storage protein FTH1, while downregulating ACSL4). Its antiferroptotic effects were mimicked by the specific inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) and abolished by the inducer Erastin (Era). Collectively, this study suggests that OA protects against DN potentially through modulating the NRF2/HO-1 axis to mitigate ferroptosis, supporting its potential as a promising bioactive dietary compound for the management of DN.

title: Computational screening and nanodelivery of Carya cathayensis-derived peptide DFR for targeted suppression of neuroinflammation via iNOS/NF-kappaB/MAPK pathways.
authors: Liu, Kexin; He, Yanling; Li, Shasha; Tao, Han; Wei, Liang; Huang, Jianqin; Jiang, Chenyu; Farag, Mohamed A; Song, Lili; Gao, Fei
abstract: Neuroinflammation, a critical innate immune response in the central nervous system (CNS), is closely associated with dysregulated inflammatory pathways. Targeting key mediators such as inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and the NF-kappaB/MAPK signaling axis offers a promising strategy for mitigating inflammatory cascades. In this study, three novel peptides derived from Carya cathayensis (DFR, GAR, NAK) were computationally screened via molecular docking and dynamics simulations for their iNOS inhibitory potential. DFR demonstrated superior binding affinity and stability, validated through in vitro assays where it significantly suppressed LPS-induced nitric oxide (NO) and pro-inflammatory cytokine (IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, IL-6) production in BV2 microglia. To enhance therapeutic efficacy, DFR was engineered into a nanostructured delivery system (pADFR) through conjugation with a targeting ligand and PEGylation. In vivo evaluations revealed that pADFR alleviated LPS-induced behavioral deficits and reduced inflammatory mediators in mice, with mechanistic studies highlighting its suppression of NF-kappaB/MAPK pathway activation. This study underscores the potential of peptide-based nanostructures for targeted modulation of neuroinflammatory pathways, offering a platform for precision therapeutic development.

title: DksA regulates intestinal colonization of Klebsiella pneumoniae through metabolic plasticity.
authors: Wan, Jia; Wang, Yixuan; Wang, Lin; Li, Yaxin; Xiong, Shun; Chu, Xiakun; Zhou, Dianrong; Li, Jiachen; Li, Meisong; Xia, Xue; Wang, Wenli; Yang, Meiting; Liu, Weiqing; Wen, Yiwu; Qiu, Zhilang; Feng, Siyuan; Tian, Guo-Bao
abstract: Intestinal colonization by Klebsiella pneumoniae is recognized as a pivotal prerequisite for its systemic dissemination and subsequent invasive infection; however, the metabolic basis and regulatory mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. In this study, we employed transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-seq) to systematically identify metabolic genes associated with intestinal colonization in K. pneumoniae. By integrating high-throughput screening with in vivo phenotypic validation, we identified the global transcriptional regulator DksA as a key factor that markedly enhances K. pneumoniae intestinal colonization. Mechanistically, DksA may contribute to intestinal colonization through modulation of central carbon metabolism. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, together with homology modeling and molecular dynamics simulations, suggested that DksA may contribute to allosteric remodeling of key RNA polymerase structural domains, thereby influencing the expression of metabolic genes, carbon source utilization, and intestinal colonization by K. pneumoniae. Collectively, our findings highlight the important role of metabolic plasticity associated with transcriptional regulation in K. pneumoniae intestinal colonization and provide a theoretical framework and potential targets for developing anti-colonization strategies that exploit pathogen metabolic vulnerabilities. IMPORTANCE: Intestinal colonization is a critical first step in the pathogenesis and transmission of Klebsiella pneumoniae, yet the bacterial factors that support persistence in the gut remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identified the transcriptional regulator DksA as an important contributor to intestinal colonization through genome-wide genetic screening and in vivo validation. Multi-omics analyses suggest that DksA is associated with the regulation of bacterial carbon metabolism and metabolic adaptation, processes that are likely important for survival in the nutrient-variable intestinal environment. Structural modeling further provides insight into how DksA may influence transcriptional regulation. These findings expand our understanding of the factors that facilitate K. pneumoniae gut colonization and highlight bacterial metabolic adaptation as a potential target for strategies aimed at limiting colonization and subsequent infection.

title: Variant-informed multimodal tissue-state modeling reveals an NRF2 stress niche and dependency axis in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered cancer.
authors: Kong, Mowei; Li, Qiuing; Zhao, Xingwei; Wang, Yu; Luo, Yamei; Yu, Yang; Zhang, Chunxiang
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cancer genotypes influence transcriptional programs, spatial organization, histopathology, and treatment-response states, yet these molecular and tissue-level features are often analyzed separately in public-data studies. VISTA was developed as a variant-informed, multimodal framework for modeling genotype-linked tissue states and prioritizing validation-ready biological hypotheses. METHODS: VISTA integrates somatic variants, protein-region and AlphaMissense-informed priors, RNA-state scoring, whole-slide image embeddings, immunotherapy cohorts, spatial and single-cell references, cell-line dependency maps, and pharmacogenomic screens. We evaluated the framework in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered lung cancer and melanoma, using the NRF2 stress axis as a biologically defined test case. Analyses incorporated project-adjusted modeling, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation testing, leave-project sensitivity analyses, independent tumor-level validation cohorts, fixed-effect external meta-analysis, model-system analyses using DepMap/CCLE, tissue-context analyses, immunotherapy cohorts, and exploratory whole-slide image analyses. RESULTS: In TCGA LUAD, LUSC, and SKCM pilot cohorts, KEAP1 and NFE2L2 alterations were consistently associated with NRF2 stress activation across project-adjusted models and sensitivity analyses. Independent analyses of CPTAC LUAD, CPTAC LSCC, and non-TCGA LUAD cohorts reproduced higher NRF2-state scores in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered tumors. Fixed-effect external meta-analysis supported associations with both KEAP1 mutation and combined KEAP1-or-NFE2L2 alteration status. DepMap/CCLE analyses provided complementary model-system evidence: KEAP1/NFE2L2-mutant models had higher NRF2 scores, while NRF2-high or KEAP1/NFE2L2-mutant contexts showed stronger NFE2L2 dependency. Tissue-context analyses positioned NRF2 stress near hypoxic, stromal, myeloid, and immune programs. Immunotherapy cohorts supported the relevance of NRF2-associated states to treatment-response biology, while also indicating limited utility for static pan-cancer prediction. Exploratory whole-slide image analyses using pathology foundation-model embeddings identified morphology associations with myeloid, hypoxic, and CAF/TGF-beta barrier programs. DISCUSSION: VISTA provides an evidence-layered approach to variant-informed tissue-state modeling. By integrating genomic, transcriptomic, imaging, spatial, cellular, dependency, and pharmacogenomic evidence, it can help prioritize genotype-linked cancer states and validation-ready hypotheses. VISTA is not intended to function as a stand-alone clinical predictor; its claims are bounded by the evidence available in each data layer and by the biological and clinical context of the analyzed cohorts.

title: Chaihu-Guizhi Decoction Attenuates Airway Remodelling in COPD Mice via the TGF-beta1/Smads Signalling Pathway: An Integrated Proteomic and Metabolomic Analysis.
authors: Yu, Jiuwang; Wu, Xiaodong; Chen, Zeyu; Zhai, Chenxu; A, Jinxiang; Zhang, Yuping
abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterised by persistent airway injury and remodelling, and the mechanisms by which Chai-Hu-Gui-Zhi Decoction (CGD) acts in COPD remain unclear. This study investigated whether CGD attenuates airway remodelling through the TGF-beta1/Smads-EMT-ECM signalling axis. A mouse COPD model was established by cigarette-smoke exposure plus intranasal lipopolysaccharide. After model induction, mice received dexamethasone acetate or low-, medium- or high-dose CGD for 28 days. UHPLC-MS/MS, network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, proteomics, metabolomics, ELISA, western blotting, RT-PCR, pulmonary function testing and histopathology were integrated. CGD dose-dependently improved pulmonary function and lung pathology and reduced BALF total protein, NO, VEGF, IFN-gamma, MPO, CXCL1 and serum 8-OHdG. Multi-omics and network analyses implicated phenylalanine/tyrosine/tryptophan biosynthesis, the histidine-glutamate-hypoxanthine axis, MAPK, PI3K-Akt and TGF-beta1-related pathways. Validation showed that CGD decreased TGF-beta1, p-SMAD2/3, SMAD2/3, MMP-9 and TIMP-1; increased SMAD7 and E-cadherin; and regulated Smad2/Smad3/Smad7 mRNA. CGD may attenuate COPD airway remodelling, in association with suppressed TGF-beta1/Smads signalling, restored SMAD7-mediated feedback, limited EMT and rebalanced ECM remodelling.

title: Cinchonidine Ameliorates Traumatic Brain Injury-Related Neurobehavioral Deficits via the SRC/RAF1/NF-kappaB Pathway to Attenuate Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
authors: Tang, Han; Huang, Jianchao; Sun, Caixia
abstract: Cinchonidine (CD), a metabolite derived from gut microbiota, shows promise in protecting against traumatic brain injury (TBI), where mitochondrial dysfunction is a key driver of secondary damage. Using a mouse model of controlled cortical impact (CCI) and an in vitro primary neuron injury model, CD administration resulted in improved physiological status (weight recovery, stabilized heart rate) and behavioral outcomes (increased travel distance and speed) in TBI mice. Histological analysis showed reduced hippocampal neuronal damage, decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin‑1beta, interleukin‑6, and tumor necrosis factor‑alpha), and upregulated blood-brain barrier tight-junction proteins (Claudin-5, Occludin, zonula occludens‑1). Mitochondrial function was improved, evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA copy number, elevated expression of translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 and cytochrome c oxidase subunit IV, and restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential. In addition, CD attenuated TBI-induced changes in mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis, restoring the phosphorylated dynamin-related protein 1 (p-DRP1)/DRP1 ratio and the expression of mitofusin 1/2 (MFN-1/2) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1alpha), while reducing mitochondrial DRP1. Network pharmacology identified proto‑oncogene tyrosine‑protein kinase Src (SRC) as a key target, validated by stable binding in molecular docking and drug affinity responsive target stability assays. Furthermore, cellular thermal shift assays demonstrated a direct interaction between CD and SRC. CD treatment suppressed the activation of the SRC/RAF proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein kinase (RAF1)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kappaB) signaling axis, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of SRC and p65, along with decreased expression of RAF1 and cleaved Caspase-3. Crucially, SRC knockdown mimicked CD's protection, while SRC overexpression abolished its benefits. These findings suggest that CD ameliorates post-TBI mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and neuronal damage by inhibiting SRC kinase activity and its downstream RAF1/NF-kappaB signaling pathway. Thus, CD may represent a promising SRC-targeted neuroprotective strategy for TBI.

title: A gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene score for subtyping and predicting the treatment response in rheumatoid arthritis: integrative analysis with in silico knockout validation.
authors: Sun, Xiang-Fei; Yang, Yi-Jie; Li, Chen-Long; Huang, Tai; Wang, Qi; Yu, Qi
abstract: BACKGROUND: The pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) involves a complex interplay between immune dysregulation and metabolic disturbance, with the gut microbiota and its metabolites playing pivotal roles. However, integrated biomarkers based on the "gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene" regulatory axis that can quantify its impact on RA stratification and therapeutic response are lacking. METHODS: We integrated multiple RA transcriptomic datasets to screen for host genes explicitly associated with the gut microbiota and metabolites using the gutMGene database. A gut microbiota-metabolite-host score (GMS) was constructed via principal component analysis (PCA). Immune infiltration patterns were evaluated using CIBERSORT. Furthermore, scRNA-seq was employed to map the cellular origins of key genes, and in silico knockout analysis using scTenifoldKnk was performed to simulate the functional ablation of core host genes within this regulatory axis. Additionally, molecular docking was conducted to validate the binding affinities between the key host proteins and the optimal small molecule. RESULTS: We identified seven microbiota-metabolite-host hub genes (FOS, JUN, IDO1, PEMT, EGFR, ABCC4, and FADS3) and constructed the GMS. The GMS stratified patients with RA into two distinct functional subtypes: an adaptive immune activation subtype and an inflammatory-metabolic composite subtype. Notably, the GMS demonstrated superior performance in predicting responses to anti-TNF and rituximab therapies. The scRNA-seq analysis revealed high expression of FOS and JUN in T cells and NK cells. In silico knockout analysis further revealed the central transcription factors FOS and JUN as key executors of this axis, as their ablation significantly affected osteoclast differentiation and the enrichment of TNF/MAPK inflammatory pathways. These computational findings support the core mechanism by which gut microbiota-metabolite signalling drives RA joint pathology via FOS/JUN. Molecular docking results confirmed strong binding interactions between the identified active molecules and their respective target proteins. CONCLUSION: This study establishes a GMS based on the gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene regulatory axis as a robust tool for molecular subtyping and predicting biological therapy responses in patients with RA. Crucially, through integrated computational modelling, including in silico knockout and molecular docking validation, we identified FOS/JUN as critical executor genes linking the gut microenvironment to RA bone destruction, providing novel targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at the gut-joint axis.

title: Mononuclear Mg(ii) and Ca(ii) metallocarboxylates of N-phthaloyl-gamma-aminobutyric acid: synthesis, characterization, ds-DNA binding, preliminary anticancer evaluation against MDA-MB-231 cells, and computational studies.
authors: Abbas, Naeem; Arfan, Muhammad; Iqbal, Yasir; Iqbal, Mudassir; Ahmed, Naeem; Alharbi, Mona G; Gatasheh, Mansour K
abstract: This study reports the synthesis of neurotransmitter-inspired, biolabile mononuclear Mg(ii)/(NY1) and Ca(ii)/(NY2) metallocarboxylates of N-phthaloyl-gamma-aminobutyric acid ligand (NPGABA), motivated by the growing relevance of metallocarboxylates in addressing essential metal-ion deficiencies. Extensive spectral (i.e. IR, UV-vis, (1)H-NMR, (13)C-NMR, AAS, and ICP-AES) and analytical (SEM, micro-analysis and thermal gravimetric analysis) techniques were used to characterize and confirm the formation of the ligand and its metal carboxylate complexes. The complexes were confirmed to have the formulas [Mg(NPGABA)(2)(H(2)O)(2)](4) (NY1) and [Mg(NPGABA)(2)(H(2)O)(4)] (NY2), where NPGABA is the abbreviation of the ligand in its deprotonated form. The DNA-binding interactions of the NPGABA ligand (NY0) and its alkaline earth metal carboxylate complexes with magnesium (Mg/NY1) and calcium (Ca/NY2) were investigated through a combination of biophysical, computational, and biological assays. UV-visible absorption studies revealed a significant hyperchromic effect without a bathochromic/hypsochromic shift, indicative of a non-intercalative external binding mode (i.e., minor groove binding or electrostatic interaction with the anionic sugar phosphate backbone of DNA). Binding constants (K (b)) were calculated by UV-vis spectroscopy at a temperature of 310.15 K and pH of 7.4 as 2.18 x 10(5) M(-1) (NY0), 4.05 x 10(5) M(-1) (NY1), and 4.21 x 10(5) M(-1) (NY2), with Gibbs free energies (DeltaG degrees ) of -31.68, -33.28, and -33.38 kJ mol(-1), respectively, confirming spontaneous interactions. Similarly, fluorescence emission spectroscopic studies demonstrated eminent quenching without any shift, providing complementary evidence for the presence of external non-intercalative interactions. Accordingly, the binding constants (K (b)) calculated by this technique under the same physiological conditions were 1.2 x 10(4) M(-1) (NY0), 4.41 x 10(4) M(-1) (NY1), and 8.61 x 10(4) M(-1) (NY2), with binding site numbers of 0.86 (NY0), 0.95 (NY1), and 1.01 (NY2) and Gibbs free energies (DeltaG degrees ) of -24.23, -27.56, and -29.27 kJ mol(-1), respectively, confirming the spontaneity of the interaction process. Molecular docking simulations against the canonical B-DNA (PDB: 1BNA) and the aromatase cytochrome P450 enzyme (PDB: 3EQM) also supported the occurrence of non-intercalative external binding interactions, with NY2 demonstrating the most favorable binding pose and energy. This non-intercalative external binding interaction was further endorsed by minute perturbation in the DNA solution viscosity and analogical consistency with classical groove binders like netropsin and distamycin A (K (b)  approximately  10(5)-10(7) M(-1)). The observed DNA binding affinity trend (NY2 > NY1 > NY0) has a direct correlation with the cytotoxic potency of the investigated compounds against triple negative breast cancer cells (MDA-MB-231). This consolidated investigation proved NY2 as a non-intercalative DNA-binding small molecule with preliminary anticancer activity, offering a strategic route for developing sustainable metallocarboxylate-based therapeutics.

title: Ferroptosis-associated candidate genes in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: evidence from human peripheral blood and mouse brain.
authors: Li, Jia; Wang, Cong; Li, Hongwen; Liu, Yafan; Cheng, Chunchao; Zhao, Zilin; Jiang, Guifang; Cui, Xiaopeng; Ng, Ben Chat Fong; Zhao, Yan; Wu, Zhuolin; Yang, Xinyu
abstract: BACKGROUND: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) has high morbidity and mortality. Ferroptosis may contribute to aSAH-related brain injury, but its peripheral and brain-associated signatures remain unclear. METHODS: Human peripheral-blood dataset GSE36791 (43 aSAH, 18 controls) was analyzed using limma, FerrDb intersection, WGCNA, GO/KEGG enrichment, and PPI-based prioritization. qPCR validation was performed in peripheral blood from 10 aSAH patients and 10 non-SAH controls; aSAH samples were collected within 24 h after rupture. Mean ages were 60.2 +/- 7.7 and 63.6 +/- 8.9 years, with 5 and 4 males, respectively. Brain-level validation used GSE79416 mouse cortex and OMIX006611 mouse SAH single-cell RNA-seq data. Male C57BL/6 J mice (8 weeks, 20-22 g) underwent cisterna magna autologous blood injection; brain tissues were collected 1 day after SAH (n = 6/group). Immune infiltration and molecular docking were also performed. RESULTS: Among 2,645 DEGs, 35 were ferroptosis-related. MAPK3, STAT3, G6PD, and PGD were prioritized as ferroptosis-associated candidate genes and were upregulated in human aSAH peripheral blood, mouse SAH cortex, and the clinical qPCR cohort. Single-cell analysis showed expression of the corresponding mouse genes across annotated brain cell types, especially immune/glial populations. In mouse SAH brain tissue, MAPK3/ERK1, STAT3, PGD, and G6PD protein levels increased, p-STAT3/STAT3 ratio was elevated, MDA content increased, and GPX4 activity decreased. Immune profiling showed increased neutrophils, mast cells, and activated dendritic cells. Ganoderic acid A was prioritized as a preliminary in silico candidate. CONCLUSION: MAPK3, STAT3, G6PD, and PGD are ferroptosis-associated candidate genes in aSAH, supported by human peripheral-blood, mouse cortex, single-cell, and mouse brain validation. Ganoderic acid A remains an exploratory in silico candidate requiring further functional validation.

title: FUBP1 lactylation suppresses trophoblast function in fetal growth restriction.
authors: Liang, Xinyue; Yao, Shenshen; Ma, Jian; Wang, Dan
abstract: BACKGROUND: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a common complication of pregnancy; however, its exact molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Excessive lactate accumulation in the placenta is often observed during FGR. High concentrations of lactate can regulate the proliferation of pathological cells through lactylation of key proteins. Therefore, we aimed to screen key lactylation modification-related genes (LMRGs) and provide new directions for the diagnosis and treatment of FGR. METHODS: The Differentially expressed LMRGs (DE-LMRGs) in FGR were evaluated using the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Functional enrichment analysis was performed, and a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was created to explore the characteristics of placental gene networks associated with FGR. In addition, secondary cluster analysis was performed using a machine learning algorithm to screen critical genes. We evaluated the degree of immune cell infiltration of key genes using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. The expression and function of key genes in FGR were verified experimentally. Furthermore, FUBP1 lactylation was assessed using mass spectrometry and immunoprecipitation. We overexpressed wild-type and mutant FUBP1 in HTR-8/SVneo cells to investigate how its lactylation regulates trophoblast function. Finally, patient-derived organoids (PDO) were cultured to confirm the underlying mechanism of FUBP1. RESULTS: In total, 35 DE-LMRGs were identified, and their PPI network was constructed. Two distinct FGR clusters were obtained using unsupervised consensus clustering. Moreover, the DE-LMRGs between the two patterns were mainly enriched in immune cell regulation-related molecular functions. We identified 5 overlapping key genes (BCLAF1, FUBP1, S100A6, CSRP1, CSRP2) by integrating the LASSO, random forest (RF), and SVM-RFE algorithms and screening for genes with a large fold change (using log2-FC). FUBP1 and BCLAF1 expression was lower in FGR placental tissues than in normal controls. Functional assays showed that both genes typically promote HTR-8/SVneo cell proliferation and invasion. However, lactylation of FUBP1 exerted the opposite effect by inhibiting proliferation and invasion and promoting apoptosis, indicating that FUBP1 lactylation regulates trophoblast function. Furthermore, PDO derived from the trophoblast tissues of patients with FGR revealed that FUBP1 lactylation suppressed PDO formation. CONCLUSIONS: FUBP1 lactylation is identified as a novel mechanism suppressing trophoblast function in FGR. This finding expands the field of FGR research by highlighting the role of lactylation-modified proteins and provides crucial insights into the pathological mechanisms of FGR.

title: Role and mechanism of ATF6-mediated endoplasmic reticulum stress in ITLN-1 against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
authors: Liu, Yanqing; Xu, Lu; Zhang, Zhe; Zhang, Caiqin; Liu, Peijie; Li, Pan; Wang, Shuya; Tian, Ye; Yang, Yang; Niu, Xiaochen
abstract: AIMS: Intelectin-1 (ITLN-1), a novel adipocytokine, exerts neuroprotective effects against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), yet its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study focused on activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), a key endoplasmic reticulum stress sensor, to explore its role in CIRI-induced neuronal injury and determine whether ITLN-1 mediates neuroprotection through ATF6 regulation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We established an N2a cell hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) model and a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model. Using protein-protein molecular docking, in situ proximity ligation assay, Western blotting, mitochondrial membrane potential assays, and TUNEL staining, we investigated ATF6 activation in neuronal apoptosis and its upstream regulatory mechanisms. KEY FINDINGS: H/R injury markedly induced ATF6 activation in N2a cells, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction and promoting apoptosis. ATF6 overexpression further aggravated these effects, supporting its critical pathogenic role in CIRI. Mechanistic analyses revealed that ITLN-1 physically associates with ATF6. Both ITLN-1 overexpression and exogenous recombinant ITLN-1 administration significantly suppressed excessive ATF6 activation, modulated the JNK signaling pathway, improved cell viability, reduced intracellular calcium overload and reactive oxygen species accumulation, and attenuated neuronal apoptosis. In vivo, ITLN-1 ameliorated neurological deficits, reduced neuronal damage, and alleviated demyelination, whereas ITLN-1 knockdown produced opposite effects. SIGNIFICANCE: Excessive ATF6 activation underlies CIRI-induced neuronal injury. ITLN-1 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting ATF6 and modulating JNK signaling, thereby alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction and reducing apoptosis. These findings highlight the ITLN-1/ATF6 axis as a promising therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

title: KNOX-HDAC2 complex suppresses the CAND1 expression is involved in sporophytic development of Pyropia yezoensis.
authors: Yang, Xiuwen; Xu, Ling; He, Hongyan; Zeb, Aurang; Shen, Songdong
abstract: The alternation of generations is a critical developmental process in plants. Knotted1-like homeobox (KNOX) transcription factors are known to regulate cell fate and alternation of generations in land plants, while their regulatory mechanisms in basal photosynthetic eukaryotes remain elusive. Here, we characterized the PyKNOX, a highly conserved homeodomain transcription factor from the red algae Pyropia yezoensis and demonstrated its essential role in maintaining the sporophyte phase. Using affinity purification-mass spectrometry (AP-MS) alongside in vitro and in vivo interaction assays, we revealed that PyKNOX physically recruits the histone deacetylase PyHDAC2 to assemble a transcriptional repressor complex. Genome-wide binding landscape analysis via DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) identified a conserved "TGAG" core motif and highlighted a significant enrichment of target genes within the Skp1-Cullin1-F-box (SCF) ubiquitin ligase complex. Further yeast one-hybrid (Y1H), EMAS and molecular docking assays unequivocally confirmed that PyKNOX directly targets and binds to the promoter of PyCAND1, a key exchange factor in the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Spatiotemporal expression profiling demonstrated that the PyKNOX-PyHDAC2 complex is highly upregulated during the diploid sporophyte stages (free-living filaments and conchosporangial branches), showing a strong negative correlation with the PyCAND1 expression. Together, our findings propose a coordinated epigenetic and transcriptional network where the PyKNOX-PyHDAC2 complex suppresses expression of the SCF component CAND1 in sporophytic development of P.yezoensis. This study provides evolutionary insights into the genetic cascades governing life cycle transitions in red algae P. yezoensis, and offers theoretical guidance for the future nori seedling industry.

title: Exploring the bistable equilibrium of methylated CpG DNA recognition by the MBD2 protein.
authors: Volkenandt, Senta; Belyaeva, Julia; Li, Torry; Elgeti, Matthias; Metzler, Ralf; Imhof, Petra; Williams, David C Jr; Bagherpoor Helabad, Mahdi
abstract: Methyl-CpG binding domain 2 (MBD2) is a critical epigenetic regulator that selectively binds methylated CpG dinucleotides, key marks controlling gene regulation and chromatin organization. Understanding the interactions and conformational dynamics underlying this high selectivity is essential to elucidate MBD2's regulatory role. Here, using extensive classical MD simulations, we explored the formation of the MBD2-mCpG recognition complex. By initially positioning MBD2 one base pair downstream of its target, we observed its transition to the target site within microseconds. Notably, upon binding, MBD2 adopts two distinct stable conformations: a primary state closely resembling the X-ray crystal structure, and a secondary state of reduced affinity that nevertheless retains comparable selectivity for mCpG. Our results establish S189 as a key macro-switch; loss of its interaction with the methylcytosine backbone shifts the equilibrium toward the secondary state. This is corroborated by MD simulations of the S189A mutant, which preferentially adopts the secondary state-like conformation. Complementary NMR experiments confirm that S189A mutation does not alter mCpG selectivity, while fluorescence polarization measurements reveal a reduced binding affinity, consistent with our MD simulations results. Together, these findings indicate that MBD2 binding to methylated CpG involves a bistable equilibrium, providing new insights into how high affinity and adaptability are balanced in epigenetic recognition. In a broader context, our findings suggest that such alternative bound-state equilibria may represent an inherent feature of specific protein-DNA complexes.

title: Synthesis and Evaluation of Aryloxy-Acetamide Derivatives as CBX2 Inhibitors.
authors: Kawamoto, Yuichiro; Takase, Shohei; Kumar, Ashutosh; Maemoto, Yuki; Zhang, Kam Y J; Ito, Hisanaka; Ito, Akihiro
abstract: The CBX2 protein plays a key role in the methylation of histone lysine residues related to epigenetic silencing. In contrast to other polycomb paralogs, there are few examples of CBX2 modulators, which prompted us to develop small-molecule CBX2 inhibitors by synthetic evolution based on virtual screening hit scaffolds previously reported by our group. We synthesized a series of aryloxy-acetamide derivatives and evaluated their CBX2 inhibitory activities using the NanoBRET assay and the subsequent NanoBiT assay. Through structural modifications, compound 16 was identified as the best CBX2 inhibitor in this series.

title: Omics-driven improvement of safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.) for climate resilience, oil quality, and high-value metabolites under changing environments.
authors: Ali, Fawad; Ali, Arif; Nadeem, Muhammad Azhar; Baloch, Faheem Shehzad; Kurt, Cemal; Do, Manh Cuong; Yu, Ju-Kyung; Chung, Yong Suk
abstract: Safflower is an Asteraceae oilseed crop valued for its high-quality unsaturated fatty acids ( approximately 90% oleic and linoleic acids), natural floral pigments, and diverse bioactive compounds. These attributes underpin its applications in functional foods, nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals, and various industrial sectors. Safflower inherent tolerance to drought, heat, cold, and salinity positions it as a climate-resilient alternative to more temperature-sensitive oilseeds; however, omics-based research in this crop remains comparatively fragmented. This review consolidates recent advances across major omics domains. Genomics covers chromosome-scale assemblies, GWAS panels, QTL mapping, and diagnostic candidate genes for molecular breeding. Transcriptomics summarizes regulatory networks for flavonoid and oil biosynthesis, stress-responsive transcription factors (NAC, WRKY, bZIP, AP2/ERF), and seed developmental programs. The proteomics section addresses stress-inducible, therapeutic, and storage/lipid metabolic proteins linked to quality and stress adaptation. Metabolomics outlines quinochalcone and flavonoid pathway architecture, color-specific metabolic profiles, and emerging clinical and nutraceutical applications. Phenomics highlights UAV-based high-throughput phenotyping, RGB and multispectral imaging for salt and drought screening, and machine-learning-assisted germplasm authentication. Epigenomics focuses on DNA methylation and miRNA-mediated regulation. Finally, lipidomics and metagenomics consider oil authentication biomarkers, refining optimization, and microbiome-driven nutrient cycling shaping medicinally important compounds. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in multi-omics integration, CRISPR-based functional validation, genomic selection pipelines, and detailed characterization of root-shoot architecture under combined stresses. Addressing these gaps will advance mechanistic understanding of climate resilience and enable the development of stress-tolerant, high-yielding safflower cultivars with improved oil quality and bioactive profiles, thereby supporting climate-resilient production systems and high-value safflower-based products at scale.

title: Carboplatin-derived dinuclear Pt(IV) prodrug linked by 1,6-Diaminohexane: Design, synthesis, reduction chemistry, DNA interaction, and antitumor activity.
authors: Keivanshekooh, Hosein; Eslami Moghadam, Mahboube; Ghassemzadeh, Mitra; Jafarkhani, Saeed
