abstract: In this study, we investigated a new binuclear platinum(IV) prodrug using two main strategies. First, axial ligands were attached to the cancer drug carboplatin. This modification helps protect the drug from breaking down in the bloodstream and prevents unwanted reactions before it reaches cancer cells. It also allows two carboplatin units to be delivered into a cell at the same time using a single prodrug molecule. We designed, synthesized, and characterized a new binuclear Pt(IV) prodrug in which two carboplatin molecules are linked by a 1,6-diaminohexane chain. The stability and reduction behavior of this complex were studied in phosphate-buffered saline, both with and without reducing agents such as ascorbic acid (t(1/2) = 149.6 min). Its solubility and lipophilicity were also compared with those of clinically used platinum drugs, and theoretical calculations were used to study the reduction mechanism. DNA-binding studies showed that the Pt(IV) complex mainly interacts with DNA via groove binding (K(b) = 1441.8 M(-1)), which was confirmed by spectral monitoring, viscosity measurement, and molecular docking simulations. The biological activity of the new complex was tested on human breast cancer (MCF-7), ovarian cancer (Skov-3), and noncancerous (MCF-10 A) cell lines. The binuclear Pt(IV) prodrug showed higher anticancer activity (IC(50) = 33 muM) and greater intracellular accumulation (5.16 mug/million cell) than carboplatin (IC(50) = 67 muM and 1.68 mug/million cell). In vitro studies showed that this complex induces cancer cell death primarily through apoptosis, is associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels (36.1%), and leads to cell cycle arrest at the G1/S checkpoint in MCF-7 cells. Western blot analysis demonstrated that the binuclear Pt(IV) prodrug increased Bax expression while decreasing Bcl-2 expression, consistent with involvement of mitochondrial apoptotic signaling. Furthermore, the binuclear Pt(IV) prodrug effectively inhibited tumor growth in a breast tumor-bearing mouse model without inducing significant body weight loss, supporting its promising in vivo antitumor activity and favorable tolerability. Overall, this research provides important guidance for designing new binuclear Pt(IV) prodrugs based on clinical Pt drugs to develop cancer treatments effectively.

title: Network organization of protein binding-site landscapes across scales
authors: G. Giordano; A. Chernomoretz
abstract: Studying protein binding sites helps explain ligand recognition and selectivity, informing drug development and repurposing. Here, we combine protein language model embeddings with network analysis to investigate how local recognition environments organize across scales. We represented 121,673 non-redundant, experimentally identified binding sites using ProtT5 embeddings of ligand-contacting residues and constructed a mutual nearest-neighbor network. Embedding proximity was associated with local structural similarity, supporting the structural relevance of network relationships. Globally, the network exhibited ligand-related organization. At the mesoscopic scale, communities revealed heterogeneous landscapes within established protein classifications, with InterPro categories ranging from compact neighborhoods to dispersed recognition environments. Focusing on kinases, a major class of drug targets, we found that communities within individual proteins distinguished separate binding regions and resolved recurrent residue-defined microenvironments within broad structural classes. Local similarities also connected sites in proteins with low sequence identity and non-overlapping InterPro annotations, suggesting shared recognition features across distant proteins. Together, these results show how network organization captures both diversification within protein categories and local similarities across their boundaries. This multiscale framework complements conventional protein classifications and provides a basis for prioritizing structural and biochemical investigations of ligand cross-reactivity, selectivity, and repurposing opportunities.

title: Histone modifications directly modulate transcription factor binding to nucleosomes
authors: Luca Mariani; Martha L Bulyk
abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) that can recognize specific DNA sequences within nucleosomes play key roles in regulating cell fate transitions, but what regulates their condition-dependent binding to nucleosomes remains poorly understood. Here, we determined the direct effects of H3K27ac, H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 on binding by 7 human TFs to a highly diverse library of nucleosomes. We found that these marks influence the preference of FOXA1 and PAX7 to bind as monomers versus dimers to nucleosomes. Furthermore, H3K27ac impairs TF binding at internal regions of nucleosomes, enhancing end-binding preferences, for most of the assayed TFs. Our results suggest that histone marks represent an additional layer of cis-regulatory encoding that directly regulates TF interactions with nucleosomal binding sites.

title: A pan-cancer catalog of mutagenesis at transcription factor binding sites
authors: Harshit Sahay; Yuncheng Duan; Raluca Gordân
abstract: Transcription factor (TF) binding can contribute to mutagenesis by altering DNA damage formation or interfering with DNA repair. Although these effects have been characterized for selected TFs and mutagenic processes, their prevalence across TFs and cancer types remains poorly understood. A systematic characterization of mutation enrichment at TF binding sites is needed to guide mechanistic studies and improve the interpretation of noncoding mutations in cancer. Here, we analyzed somatic mutations from over 4,000 tumors across 15 tissue types to generate a pan-cancer catalog of mutation patterns at binding sites for 655 TFs, organized into 276 motif clusters. We assessed mutation enrichment at single-nucleotide resolution, accounting for sequence-dependent and local variation in background mutation rates. Nearly one third of <TF- cluster, tissue> pairs with sufficient mutation counts showed significant enrichment at one or more binding site positions. Enrichment was most widespread in melanoma but was detected in all 15 tissue types, with the affected TFs and binding site positions varying across tissues. Highly expressed TFs were more likely to show enrichment than lowly expressed TFs, consistent with a role for TF binding in increased mutagenesis at the binding sites. Mutational signature analysis implicated processes beyond UV damage, including age-associated processes, deamination lesions, oxidative damage, and tobacco exposure, as potentially contributing to TF-induced mutagenesis. Together, these findings suggest that diverse interactions between TF binding, DNA damage, and DNA repair may contribute to mutation enrichment in regulatory DNA. Our pan-cancer catalog reveals position-specific enrichment of somatic mutations at TF binding sites across all 15 tissue types analyzed. By identifying specific TFs and binding site positions enriched for somatic mutations, together with potential mutagenic processes acting at these positions, our study provides a roadmap for experimental assessment of TF-induced mutagenesis and informs the interpretation and prioritization of non-coding mutations in cancer.

title: Direct engagement of mycobacterial RadA by c-di-AMP at a non-catalytic site suppresses its DNA-stimulated ATPase activity
authors: Shreya Shree; Shanavas P Greeshma; Kulhar Nitin; Eerappa Rajakumara
abstract: Cyclic di-adenosine monophosphate couples DNA damage sensing to genome maintenance in mycobacteria, but how it regulates homologous recombination machinery beyond RecA remains unclear. Using Mycobacterium smegmatis RadA (MsRadA) as a model, we show by isothermal titration calorimetry that c-di-AMP binds to MsRadA, providing biophysical evidence for an interaction previously inferred only from genetic studies. C-di-AMP binding is independent of magnesium ions and is not affected by prior occupancy of the ATP-binding site by the ATP analogue β,γ-methylene adenosine 5′-triphosphate, indicating that c-di-AMP binds at a site distinct from the canonical ATPase pocket. Functionally, c-di-AMP reduces MsRadA DNA-dependent ATPase activity. Structural modelling and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations show that c-di-AMP is stably bound in the central channel of the RadA hexamer, non-covalently engaged with the DNA-binding residues Arg197, Lys226, and Arg234, which are contributed by two adjacent subunit interfaces of the hexamer. In the modelled RadA-ATP-c-di-AMP-DNA quaternary complex, c-di-AMP was predicted at a peripheral site near, but distinct from, the ATP-binding pocket. Together, these findings identify RadA as a direct physical target of c-di-AMP within the homologous recombination pathway and provide a framework for testing how c-di-AMP regulates RadA during DNA damage.

title: DeepD enables efficient genome modeling and controllable long-context sequence generation across domains of life
authors: Lai J; Xin B; Wang Z; Yu A; Chen Z; Guo Y; Zhang M; Hu B; Ye C; Chen J; Liu Q; Zhao H; Song W; Dong N; Yang F; Yang Q; Zhao H
abstract: Genome foundation models hold great potential for advancing biological research, but modeling diverse complex genomes and generating controllable genome-scale sequences remain challenging. We present DeepD, a phylogeny-informed sparse mixture-of-experts model operating at single-nucleotide resolution over a 1-million-token context while reducing active computation. Pretrained on unselected whole-genome sequences across all domains of life, DeepD learns genic and intergenic sequence features and supports broad sequence-to-function prediction across species. DeepD performs well in human protein fitness and disease variants effect prediction, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, with particular strength in regulatory regions, such as promoter and transcription-factor binding sites. Expert routing captures exon-intron boundaries, transposable elements, and distal cis-regulatory elements. DeepD also generates experimentally validated core promoters with specified transcriptional strengths. Finally, the Context-Anchor-Body strategy enables generation of complete yeast chromosome sequences and megabase-scale Arabidopsis segments, preserving gene structure and order while introducing variations within natural ranges. Together, DeepD is an efficient genome foundation model that unifies accurate sequence-to-function prediction with controllable genome-scale generation, advancing predictive and generative design of complex genomes.

title: Engineered proteins to restore and enhance neurotransmitter release
authors: Chin M; Yang K; Lopez RC; Tan C; Kaeser PS
abstract: Synapse dysfunction is a hallmark feature of many neurological diseases. Synaptic transmission is initiated in nerve terminals, where active zone protein complexes control vesicle fusion for neurotransmitter release. Here, we engineer proteins that mediate active zone functions and demonstrate their use for reconstituting and strengthening neurotransmission. A protein composed of CaVβ4 and the RIM1 zinc finger, β4-Zn, restored neurotransmitter release after active zone disruption through recruitment of Munc13. We develop β4-MC, derived from the Munc13-1 MUN and C2C domains, which bypasses Munc13 recruitment and directly mediates vesicle docking, priming and fusion after active zone disruption. In β4-MC, MUN domain functions are dispensable for docking, but active MUN and C2C domains are both necessary for neurotransmitter release. In wild-type mouse and human neurons, β4-MC but not β4-Zn strengthens neurotransmitter release. Furthermore, β4-Zn and β4-MC restore and enhance dopamine release in the mouse striatum, respectively. Hence, β4 proteins are engineered secretory proteins with therapeutic potential as enhancers of synaptic function.

title: Reconstructing human gene regulatory evolution using deep learning
authors: Yamada T; Yuan X; Zeberg H; Soltys V; Lana Alberro M; Sarropoulos I; Paabo S; Kaessmann H
abstract: Understanding the genetic changes that drove the evolution of human-specific traits is a central goal in biology. Changes in gene expression are thought to be a major source of phenotypic innovations, but identifying the underlying changes in cis-regulatory elements (CREs) along the human lineage has been difficult: functional data from great apes are scarce and unobtainable for extinct hominins, and pinpointing causal substitutions requires knowing which sequences determine CRE activity. Here, we used AlphaGenome, a sequence-to-function deep-learning model, to predict the cis-regulatory effects of ~17 million single-nucleotide substitutions specific to the human lineage and traced their consequences for gene expression evolution across 305 tissues and cell types. The 71,345 predicted cis-regulatory gains lie mostly outside human accelerated regions and arose either through creation of new CREs or, more often, through co-option of CREs ancestrally accessible in other tissues. They are also enriched for distal enhancers and for target gene functions characteristic of the corresponding tissues, suggesting that they contributed to the evolution of tissue-specific biology in humans. Genes linked to more gains were more likely to be upregulated in humans, and in silico reversion to ancestral alleles traced such upregulations to individual substitutions creating transcription factor binding motifs. Comparison with Neandertal and Denisovan genomes revealed that nearly all gains now fixed in humans predate the split from archaic hominins, yet a few modern-human-specific gains contribute substantially to gene upregulation. Our study provides a genome-wide, tissue-resolved map of cis-regulatory changes and their contribution to gene expression evolution along the human lineage.

title: Binding Mode of the Heterocyclic Amine 2-Amino-9H-pyrido[2,3-b] indole (AαC) to DNA Elucidated by Molecular Docking and Molecular Dynamics Simulation
authors: Gurudeeban Selvaraj; Satyavani Kaliamurthi; Gilles H. Peslherbe; Dong-qing Wei
abstract: Background: 2-Amino-9H-pyrido[2,3-b]indole (AαC) is a mutagenic and carcinogenic heterocyclic aromatic amine formed by pyrolysis of proteins in cooked meat and present in tobacco smoke. After metabolic activation to a reactive nitrenium ion, it modifies DNA covalently, mainly at guanine. How AαC first associates with DNA, before any covalent bond forms, is not well understood. Methods: We docked AαC to three B-DNA dodecamers (PDB IDs 1BNA, 2Z2G and 2HKC) with PatchDock and FireDock, and ran explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the docked complexes in NAMD 2.13 with the CHARMM36 force field (1BNA: 10 ns; 2Z2G: 50 ns; NPT, 300 K, 0.15 M NaCl). Results: AαC bound in the minor groove of all three dodecamers, with global binding energies of -50.08 (1BNA), -53.41 (2Z2G) and -45.22 kcal/mol (2HKC). Atomic van der Waals terms contributed -16.41 to -18.36 kcal/mol, and single hydrogen bonds to thymine, guanine or adenine oxygen atoms were identified (2.2–2.8 Å). In the simulations AαC remained bound with a low, stable backbone RMSD, whereas the DNA backbone fluctuated considerably more. The minor-groove poses were poorly oriented for covalent attack when the base pairs were intact and canonical. Conclusions: Neutral AαC forms stable, groove-bound non-covalent complexes with B-DNA, but these complexes do not by themselves position the amine for C8-guanine adduct formation. Local distortion of the DNA, or the charged nitrenium ion, may be required. The complexes presented here serve as starting structures for ongoing quantum-mechanical studies of nitrenium ion stability and covalent adduct formation.

title: The eventful journey of a ligand in and out of the binding site
authors: Alessandro Berselli; Michele Parrinello
abstract: The route a ligand follows to reach and leave a protein binding site typically involves complex molecular mechanisms that shape its efficacy as a biologically active compound. These mechanisms are reflected in the binding and unbinding kinetics, which often predict biological activity better than binding affinity alone, yet their calculation remains a bottleneck in ligand characterization. Here, we propose an approach that combines committor-based enhanced sampling with spectral analysis of the infinitesimal generator to characterize in detail how a ligand reaches the binding site of a protein and is eventually expelled. Applied to the paradigmatic benzamidine (BEN)–trypsin complex and the congeneric para-amino benzamidine (PAB), this framework reveals distinct and multifaceted binding pathways for the two ligands, uncovering a previously uncharacterized BEN binding site that competes with the crystallographic site, while identifying a common rotational bottleneck for unbinding. The computed unbinding free energies closely agree with experimental measurements. The spectral decomposition of the infinitesimal generator provides access to the slow dynamical modes of the system. From the slowest mode, we derive residence times and kinetic rate constants that agree with available experimental data and with independent OPES flooding simulations, while requiring substantially less computational effort. This approach offers a privileged perspective to resolve the complexity of protein–ligand binding-unbinding process, with potential applications to ligand screening and the characterization of multiple binding sites.
